subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: changing plan when the situation shifts [Revision]
passage: Arohi and I had planned to go to the river-cleaning rally on Sunday; she had even printed a banner. I'm Sabina, her classmate, and I was at her flat at breakfast when she went quiet over the local news. “Gathering has turned tense,” she read out. “Officials say the crowd is far bigger than expected.” She put her phone down. “I don't think we should go.” I reminded her that we'd made a plan. “The plan was for a peaceful morning,” she said. She texted her aunt to cancel the lift, then messaged the eco club: “Can I help with the awareness table in the colony park instead?” By noon she was folding leaflets, humming. I'd guess she was a bit disappointed, but she never said so.

qa.q: What did Arohi read on the news at breakfast?
qa.a: That the gathering had turned tense and the crowd was bigger than expected.

qa.q: What does Arohi's humming while folding leaflets suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: That she felt settled about the new decision, though Sabina guesses Arohi may also have been a little disappointed.

qa.q: What else could Arohi do to judge the risk, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a trusted adult to read the latest updates with her, because a second view helps her judge whether it is safe; the awareness table already let her help without the tense crowd.

qa.q: How might Arohi's aunt see the cancelled lift?
qa.a: The aunt probably sees a careful teen changing plans sensibly and is relieved that Arohi is staying away from the tension.

grounding: A teen drops a planned protest when news says it is tense and joins a peaceful awareness activity instead.

passage:
Wednesday: Santosh had planned it for a week. Saturday's gathering outside the district office for cleaner drinking water in the town's schools: peaceful, permitted, and his parents had agreed he could go with his friend Lalremsiami and her father.

Saturday, 10 am: As they were putting on their shoes, Lalremsiami's father read out a local news update. The gathering had grown tense; some outsiders had started pushing at the barricades, and police were asking people to disperse. Santosh felt a pang. He'd made a poster. He'd told everyone.

"The situation has changed," he said slowly. "We said peaceful. It's not anymore." They stayed home.

The next Saturday: Santosh and Lalremsiami set up a small table outside their school with water-testing strips borrowed from the science lab, showing parents the results from three school taps. Forty parents signed a letter to the district office.

qa.q: How many parents signed the letter?
qa.a: Forty parents signed a letter to the district office.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when he heard the news update?
qa.a: Santosh felt a pang of disappointment, having made a poster and told everyone, but he accepted the change.

qa.q: What else could Santosh do if the gathering is held again peacefully?
qa.a: He could check the news and the organisers' updates on the morning itself, and go only if it is calm, with the same adult and exit plan.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami's father see Santosh's decision?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and respectful, seeing Santosh change the plan based on new information without arguing.

grounding: Shows a teen deciding not to attend when reports say a gathering has turned tense, and instead helping with a peaceful awareness activity.

passage:
Reena, beta, you're upset your rally was cancelled? Sit. Your Noor nani has a story.

When I was sixteen, in Aligarh, I was all set to march with the girls from my school for a proper bus stop outside our gate. Banners made, songs practised. My ammi even agreed.

That morning the milkman told us the crowd near the collectorate had turned angry. Stones had been thrown. Some strangers had joined who weren't students at all.

I stood at the door with my banner, and my heart sank. But I thought: we planned a peaceful march. This isn't that anymore.

So I stayed back. The next week, my friends and I went door to door in our lane with a paper, explaining why the bus stop mattered. We got a hundred and twenty signatures. The bus stop came two years later, but it came.

qa.q: How many signatures did the girls get?
How did young Noor feel standing at the door with her banner?
qa.a: Young Noor's heart sank with disappointment after all the preparation, yet Noor felt clear that the march was no longer peaceful.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what might have happened otherwise?
qa.a: The milkman's news was the turning point; if she had gone anyway, she could have been caught in a crowd that had turned angry.

qa.q: How might young Noor's ammi have felt when she stayed back?
qa.a: Her ammi probably felt relieved and proud, seeing her daughter make a careful choice on her own.

grounding: An elder recalls deciding not to join a march after hearing it had turned tense, and working on a peaceful signature drive instead.
